We sincerely thank all reviewers for their thoughtful feedback and constructive suggestions. It has significantly improved our work.

We hope we have addressed all reviewer comments in our rebuttal and follow-up responses. We have also addressed Reviewer 4qiP’s comments via the Author Comments option. It has been posted directly below our rebuttal. We hope this will help clarify the follow-up questions.

Please find the summary of the paper’s rebuttal process:

**Major Revisions:**
1. We have conducted comprehensive significance testing and will include the same in the camera-ready version
2. We have benchmarked the performance of contact PPG + contact resp + blink for cognitive load estimation and will include it as a baseline comparison
3. We have conducted the following experiments and will include them in the camera-ready version:
    - Cross-validation results
    - Elucidation of the NASA-TLX survey and our decision to binarize the scores
    - Complete model descriptions and implementation details
    - Explanation of the correlation between vital signs and cognitive load
    - Dataset details pertaining to timestamps and ECG data availability
    - Add SNR & MACC, with standard deviations for all metrics
    - Explanation addressing stress and how prior work motivated our task selection for cognitive load induction

**Key Strengths Maintained:**
1. Introducing a first-of-its-kind dataset for remote estimation of cognitive load via multimodal vital sign sensing
2. A hardware sensing stack and data collection protocol designed for remote physiological sensing for both vital signs and cognitive load assessment
3. Extensive benchmarking of state-of-the-art algorithms for rPPG, remote respiration, and cognitive load estimation with comprehensive metrics

**Remaining Concerns:** As raised by Reviewer 4qiP, we acknowledge potential stress confounding as an important consideration. While we believe the effect is minimal given our experimental design and empirical label agreement, we agree that this merits further investigation. We have addressed this concern in our follow-up comment below the rebuttal and are committed to developing approaches to better disentangle cognitive load from stress.

We believe our responses have addressed the core concerns while preserving the paper’s main contributions. We are committed to incorporating all accepted suggestions into the final version. Thank you again for your valuable time and expertise in reviewing our work.

Thank you for giving us the chance to explain further.

> Clarify biosignal-cognitive load mechanisms & emphasize stress-cognitive load distinction

We will improve the camera-ready paper to discuss vital sign-cognitive load correlations with appropriate citations. We will also highlight the distinction b/w interrelated concepts of stress & cognitive load.

> My guess is that stress-related biophysical response is a stronger signal than purely cognitive induced response, so the accuracy is a bit lower. I'd want more evidence before just accepting that this difference is only due to "variability", though that will play a role

Thank you for highlighting this important nuance. We will include the analysis in our supplement. Here, we note changing from **multi-dimensional (Mental Demand + Temporal Demand + Effort + Frustration)** to **single-dimension (Mental Demand only)** labeling serves as an ablation rather than separating stress from cognitive load. Prior works [6,7] use our same multi-dimensional format. As mentioned in the rebuttal, separating cognitive load & stress requires fundamentally different tasks, which are outside our scope.

**Clarifying our ablation:** We compared our multi-dimensional approach with single-dimension labeling for deriving binary GT labels. Both use identical physiological inputs for ML training - only the target labels differ. As highlighted in the rebuttal, **>99% binary GT labels match between both approaches. Only 1 GT label differs out of 152 GT labels**. While not absolutely conclusive, the observed ~5% performance decrease with single-dimension labeling likely reflects GT variation & model stochasticity rather than measuring different physiological constructs.

**Acknowledgment of confounding factors:** We acknowledge potential stress confounding as an important consideration. While we believe the effect is minimal given our empirical label agreement, we agree this merits further investigation. We are committed to developing approaches to better disentangle cognitive load from stress.

> Hyperparameters & val set

For loss functions, the model uses contrastive loss by default (with MSE). We experimented with adding the SNR Loss, Negative Pearson Loss, and replacing MSE with MSE + KL Divergence in the contrastive loss. Upon validation, we settled on a weighted sum: Neg Pearson + SNR + modified Contrastive losses. Our supplement will include further details about hyperparams, val set & losses. **Our code lists all hyperparams and is seeded for reproducibility.** We will also release saved models for faithful reproduction.

For traditional ML models in Table 4 (RF, GB, etc.), we used conservative hyperparam tuning with widely-used default parameters known to be robust across tasks. The val set served as a sanity check to confirm standard configurations performed reasonably without overfitting, rather than for fine-grained tuning.

> Survey chronology

We will modify Fig. 3 to include the survey chronology, elucidate the protocol, and answer Q4 a & b clearly.

> Participant engagement & performance

Thank you for this critical observation. We did not establish a performance-based exclusion (e.g., 80% threshold). **As evidenced by prior work [1,2,3], when engaging with two tasks simultaneously (here, memorization & multiplication), the performance of the second task (multiplication) decrements with higher induced cognitive loads. Excluding low-performing participants would systematically remove those experiencing the highest cognitive load - the most valuable data.**

Our exclusion criteria focused on engagement, not performance [1,4,5]: participants who failed to attempt math problems, showed impossibly fast responses, or misunderstood instructions. All participants engaged genuinely and answered our validation questions correctly (e.g., 10×6=60). No recordings were dropped due to this. When participants misunderstood instructions, we restarted upon re-explaining. We will mention this exclusion criterion in the supplement. 

 ---

[1] Deck, C., et al. (2021). On the consistency of cognitive load. European Economic Review, 134, 103695.

[2] Révész, A., et al. (2016). Measuring cognitive task demands using dual-task methodology, subjective self-ratings, and expert judgments: A validation study. Studies in second language acquisition, 38(4), 703-737.

[3] Brunken, R., et al. (2003). Direct measurement of cognitive load in multimedia learning. Educational psychologist, 38(1), 53-61.

[4] Allred, S., et al. (2016). Cognitive load and strategic sophistication. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 125, 162-178.

[5] Deck, C., & Jahedi, S. (2015). The effect of cognitive load on economic decision making: A survey and new experiments. European Economic Review,78, 97-119.

[6] Wickens, C. D. (2008). Multiple resources and mental workload. Human factors, 50(3), 449-455.

[7] Young, M. S., et al. (2015). State of science: mental workload in ergonomics. Ergonomics, 58(1), 1-17.

Thanks for the detailed reply! I've added some follow-up questions/thoughts to select points. If I don't write about a point, we can consider it resolved...

> Q1 and Q2

I'm mostly satisfied with these answers. I'd recommend revising the paper to make clear why we expect mechanistic connections between biosignals and cognitive load, and to help readers know that distinguishing the inter-related concepts of stress and cognitive load is important, even if that falls a bit out of scope of this paper.

> new analysis using only the "Mental Demand" subscale for labeling. The results confirm the robustness of our original approach: the label distribution was nearly identical (76 Low/76 High originally vs. 75 Low/77 High), and the classification performance remained high (86.49% accuracy originally vs. 81.08% with Mental Demand only)

Thanks for this experiment. I'd recommend adding this to the supplement. My guess is that stress-related biophysical response is as stronger signal than purely cognitive induced response, so the accuracy is a bit lower. I'd want more evidence before just accepting that this difference is only just due to "variability", though that will play a role


> Q6. Hyperparamters & val set

I'm not clear on what you mean by "select all our loss functions", can you elaborate?

I understand Table 4 compares many models, but the way the *validation set* was used here is not clear. This needs to be clear for your work to be reproducible.

I'm not worried so much that your hyperparameter tuning could have been more extensive, but rather not knowing *how* you did any tuning at all



> how do surveys fit in chronology

I'd recommend having a more detailed figure that lays out this information cleanly for the reader. 

The same figure might also provide clean answers to Q4a, Q4b etc.


> all participants engaged in the task and gave many correct answers.

Hmm, I'd hope for a bit more detail here. 
What was the lowest correctness percentage of any participant?
Was there thought to exclude participants below, say, 80% correct? I've seen other studies establish careful exclusion criteria to make sure they were keeping subjects actually doing the work.

We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and insightful comments. We are pleased that our dataset collection and research methodology demonstrate strong adherence to ethical principles. Please find the following amendments:

---

1. A more detailed discussion around data privacy and security, particularly focusing on the methods used for anonymizing, storing, and protecting participant data 

Ans: We currently store our dataset on the Box Drive linked to our University, which is IRB-approved as a secure storage option. Based on dataset requests, we can time-gate data sharing by enabling timed access to our dataset, helping limit misuse from extended link durations. Furthermore, instructions to anonymize video for posters, presentations and publications will be clearly specified when sharing the dataset, including clear guidelines regarding which participants' faces can be used in publications.

---

2. Clarify the safeguards in place to prevent misuse of the dataset and models. 

Ans: To avoid data misuse, we propose regulating distribution via an EULA / DUA (End-User License Agreement / Data Use Agreement) for all dataset access requests. The agreement will emphasize dataset safeguarding and restrict use to non-commercial applications. We will also implement a verification process for legitimate research purposes and institutional affiliations.

---

3. A clearer acknowledgment of the limitations regarding demographic diversity. 

Ans: We thank the reviewer for this recommendation. Our supplement currently contains sections analyzing algorithmic bias effects and demographic distribution. We will strengthen our analysis and include a dedicated section addressing demographic diversity and its impact on training remote sensing models.

---

4. It might be valuable to incorporate a statement addressing the long-term societal and ethical implications.

Ans: We thank the reviewer for this recommendation. We will include a section in our camera-ready supplement addressing the long-term societal impact of remote health sensing and associated ethical implementation (privacy, data management, etc.).

1. We apologize for missing the comment in the Dataset Code. We are happy to release the model weights for more faithful reproducibility. 

2. Further, we will address the SNR, MACC, and the other mentioned comparisons, such as frame differences, motion from the tasks, in the camera-ready paper and supplement. 

3. Here is an abridged version of the SNR & MACC analysis. We will include the same in the camera-ready version.

SNR results align with rPPG fundamentals—RGB shows stronger signals due to better blood absorption compared to NIR [1]. However, NIR achieves superior MACC, indicating that deeper penetration at NIR wavelengths captures more accurate waveform morphology. Our frequency-domain training losses likely prioritized SNR over morphological fidelity. For respiratory analysis, radar maintains a higher SNR than thermal cameras. During talking, thermal SNR degrades due to partial mouth breathing. However, this does not seem to adversely affect peak frequency (RR) detection. With the MACC, however, both modalities perform similarly. We believe this reflects the inherently noisy nature of respiratory signals when performing tasks (e.g., talking). A more in-depth analysis will be presented in the camera-ready version.

[1] Magdalena Nowara, Ewa, et al. "SparsePPG: Towards driver monitoring using camera-based vital signs estimation in near-infrared." Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition workshops. 2018.

Reviewer NipV, we would like to thank you for your insightful feedback. We are pleased that our dataset & experimental deisgn were found to be effective and significant in contribution.

**Q0. Safeguards**

Ans:  The license for the dataset is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Hence, the researcher will be allowed to use it for non-commercial purposes. We will regulate the distribution via the use of an EULA (End User License Agreement) for all those who apply for the dataset access. The EULA will note the importance of safeguarding the dataset and highlight its non-commercial use.  

---

**Q1. Synchronization between multiple contact-based and contactless data streams.**

Ans: Synchronization was performed by multiprocessing, and simultaneously starting all sensors during acquisition. That is, we add barriers to wait for all sensors to activate. We also record timestamps of when the laptop received the data. Details on the latency of the sensors and properties of timestamps will be included in the camera-ready supplement.

---

**Q2. Please provide references that inspired the experimental design and the data-acquisition protocol.**

Reviewer 4qiP, we would like to thank you for your insightful feedback. We are pleased that our dataset & approach were found to be original and of potential significance.

We address the main concerns & comments below:
---
**Q1a. Rationale for estimating cognitive load from heart/respiration/eye signals**

Ans: We have summarized the correlation between the vital signs & cognitive load in the 2nd paragraph of the introduction. We can further elucidate with citations as follows:

We first establish the relationship between vital signs & cognitive load. High cognitive load activates the sympathetic nervous system, elevating heart rate & reducing heart rate variability [1,2]. Conversely, low cognitive load activates the parasympathetic nervous system, decreasing heart rate [1,2]. Cognitively demanding tasks also accelerate respiration due to increased brain oxygen demands [3]. Additionally, behavioral markers like pupillometry & blink rate correlate with cognitive load [4]. These established relationships support using heart rate, respiratory rate, & blink patterns to distinguish cognitive load levels.

**Q1b. Can these biosignals truly predict cognitive load, or do they predict confounding correlated constructs like stress**

Ans: We thank the reviewer for their insightful question about the inner workings of these constructs. Our tasks & surveys have been designed keeping in mind prior work on cognitive load analysis. We have stayed consistent with prior works that have aimed to induce only cognitive load through various means. This is achieved through controlled mental demand, temporal demand, effort, & frustration (Figure 4). Our approach follows established methodologies: Deck et al. [5] combined load-inducing tasks, such as memorization & with decision-making problems to establish their impact on performance. Others used binary grid memorization [6,7] & digit memorization [8,9] followed by gaming, problem-solving, or risk-based decisions. Our protocol incorporates these validated approaches [5,6,7,8,9]. Further, we allow adequate time for memorization & problem-solving phases, making sure the participant is not rushed.

---

**Q2. Questions about cognitive load "ground truth": (1) Is this summation approach standard in literature? (2) What's the rationale? (3) Might stress be more easily predicted by physiological measures than mental load? (4) Would results differ using only mental TLX? (5) Can the study distinguish stress from mental load without tasks designed to induce high stress/low mental work or vice versa?**

Ans: We thank the reviewer for the important methodological question. Our approach of creating a composite cognitive load score by aggregating the Mental Demand, Temporal Demand, Effort, and Frustration subscales from the NASA-TLX is a standard method in cognitive workload research [10, 11]. This method allows us to capture an aggregated view of the mental effort exerted during our tasks.

To directly address the reviewer’s concern, we conducted a new analysis using only the "Mental Demand" subscale for labeling. The results confirm the robustness of our original approach: the label distribution was nearly identical (76 Low/76 High originally vs. 75 Low/77 High), and the classification performance remained high (86.49% accuracy originally vs. 81.08% with Mental Demand only). This small performance difference is well within the range of training variability.

Finally, we agree that our protocol was not designed to differentiate stress from cognitive load, but rather to assess varying levels of cognitive demand, which is the primary focus of this work. Distinguishing these two states is an important but separate research question that falls outside our current scope.

---

**Q3. Direct contact sensor for cognitive load (EEG, fNIRs).**

Ans: Thank you for the suggestion. The reviewer was right in their assessment of the intrusiveness of these sensors. This was the reason we did not use these sensors. We will add text about these sensors to Related Works.

---

**Q4a. Are you predicting one HR/RR/blink value for each 2 min task?**

Ans: Waveform regression for rPPG & respiratory signals was trained on 10 & 20-sec video clips. For remote vital sign estimation, multiple outputs were concatenated to calculate vitals. Specifically, we use 30-sec windows for HR & 40-sec windows for RR. For cognitive load, the hand-crafted features were extracted over the full 2-mins. By using different window lengths, finer details are captured during regression, while larger windows are robust for calculating cognitive load.

**Q4b. What is assumed about the frequency/duration of each input sensor signal?**

Ans: All our recordings are 2-min long. The sampling frequency of the sensors is listed in Supplementary Section 1.2. During training, we downsample the rPPG signals to 30 Hz & resp signals to 15 Hz to reduce computational cost.

**Q4c. How exactly do you get "truth" for each input window?**

Ans: The GT sensors, namely, the pulse oximeter & chest band, capture 2-min cardiac & respiratory waveforms. From these waveforms, HR & RR values are calculated on non-overlapping 30 & 40-second windows via frequency peak detection.

**Cognitive Load**

**Q4d. What is assumed about the frequency/duration of each input sensor signal?**

Ans: The predicted 30 & 40-second windows are concatenated, & the vital sign features are calculated on the 2-min window. Each trial has a single cognitive load label obtained via the survey scores. 

**Q4e. What is the class-balance of high/low categories?**

Ans: For all participants, our thresholding categorizes “still” & ”read” as low load, & “pattern” & “number” as high load. Hence, the classes are balanced evenly, 50% low & 50% high.

**Q4f. I'd recommend a careful rewrite of Sec 4.1 & 4.2 to carefully describe in order**

Ans: We thank the reviewer for their feedback. Currently, we have elaborated on implementation details in our supplement. We will add in-depth details in the camera-ready version.

---

**Q5. Results reporting needs statistical significance testing.**

Ans: Please refer to our reply **Q8 to Reviewer NipV**

---

**Q6. Hyperparamters & val set**

Ans: Our work focused on establishing a standardized dataset and data collection protocol to demonstrate the feasibility of remote cognitive load estimation. Our two-stage pipeline separates remote vital sign extraction (Stage 1) from cognitive load est (Stage 2). For Stage 1, we did not extensively tune hyperparams. Early exploration with the val set and Contrast-Phys+ revealed that the AdamW with lr=1e-5 worked well with 50 epochs for rPPG, 100 epochs for resp. The val set is also used to select all our loss functions. With regards to Stage 2, we conducted extensive benchmarking across ML model families, as reported in Table 4. 

---

**Q7a. How do the TLX self-assessment surveys fit into the chronology of the task sequence during data collection**

Ans: The survey is taken between the trials, i.e., we pause after the 2-min recordings. As detailed in Section 3.3, rest periods are given after the “read” & “pattern” tasks. There are no surveys for rest periods & hence no cognitive load labels. The rest periods are only used for rPPG & resp regression.

**Q7b. Did you confirm that all participants actually engaged in the high-workload tasks?**

Ans: Yes, all participants engaged in the task and gave many correct answers.

---

**Q8. What is the expected ceiling in terms of how well remote cognitive load estimation? What might change if we gathered even more data from more subjects? Would we expect deep learning to outperform hand-crafted features?**

Ans: While more data would benefit all models, our key finding is that traditional ML with 25-50+ curated physiological features (RMSSD, SDNN, LF/HF ratio) consistently outperforms deep learning on our dataset due to strong inductive bias. With more data, remote sensing can approach contact-based estimation. However, the exact gap would be hard to predict.

For RR, thermal fusion performs better when more folds are included; however, the difference across the three best is still minimal. Further, a statistical significance analysis found that there is a significant difference between NIR v/s RGB and Fusion. However, for RR, the top 3 methods were found to be very similar, and the performance difference was not significant. These details and numerical values will be included for all baselines in the camera-ready version.

---

**Q2. What is the ratio of positive and negative cognitive load labels? Does it have label imbalance? Why choose a binary label setting?**

Ans: We report that the cognitive load labels in the dataset are evenly balanced, with 50% for both the positive (high load) and negative (low load) labels. Our thresholding approach labelled “still” and “read” as low load, and the two memorization tasks as high load. 

We acknowledge that cognitive load exists on a continuous spectrum. Surveys such as the NASA-TLX allow us to quantify cognitive load via a scoring system, thereby capturing the continuous nature of cognitive load. However, estimating this single numerical value for load is a challenging task and remains an ongoing research problem. Given that we present the first attempt at remote sensing of cognitive load, we simplify the task to a binary classification to prove the applicability of remote cognitive load estimation. Expanding future research to include more diverse tasks and increasing population size will enable multi-class classification and eventually regression of cognitive load scores. We will clarify the same in the camera-ready version. Here are the average survey scores (with standard deviations) for the 4 tasks:  (i) still = 4.89 (7.79) ;
(ii) read = 15.97 (14.46) ;
(iii) pattern = 48.16 (14.64) ;
(iv) number =51.16 (15.89) ;

This informs us that a binary setting would be a good choice, given the spread of the scores.

---

**Q3. The pretraining part in the paper is not clear. What is the pretrained NIR model in Sec. 4.1? The pretraining description in Sec. 6.1 (However, this gap in performance can be bridged by pretraining the NIR model using the RGB model weights) should be clarified.**

Ans: Thank you for the feedback. We have added an illustration of this pretraining in Figure 2 of the supplement. We will add more details and elucidate Sections 4.1, 4.2, and 6.1 in the camera-ready version. Here is an abridged version for reference:

We train the Contrast-Phys+ model on RGB video frames, leveraging the higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) signals in the visible spectrum to learn rich features. Since rPPG signals exhibit lower SNR in the near-infrared (NIR) spectrum, we use pretraining as a bridge: the NIR model is initialized with weights from the pretrained RGB model and then fine-tuned on NIR frames. For multimodal fusion, we prevent RGB dominance by initializing the fusion models with NIR weights. We adopt a Siamese training approach, ensuring that early network layers learn shared high-level features from both RGB and NIR modalities. These features are then fused in later stages to extract detailed rPPG signals from combined inputs. Further implementation details will be provided in the supplement with a camera-ready version.

---

**Q4. In Table 3, camera fusion and waveform fusion should be further described and clarified in the main text.**

Ans: Thank you for the feedback. We will elaborate on this in the camera-ready version. A summary of the same is as follows: 

The camera fusion model uses a Siamese architecture with the Contrast-Phys+ backbone. Unlike the rPPG approach, we do not perform any model pretraining; instead, all models are trained from scratch. For waveform fusion, we employ a simple 1D convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) that performs early fusion (1-D signals concatenation via the channel dimension) of the respiratory waveforms from thermal camera fusion and radar signals. Further implementation details will be provided in the supplement with a camera-ready version.

---

**Q5. The rPPG method and remote Resp method used in Sec. 6.2 Cognitive Load Classification should be clarified.**

Ans: We use the predicted waveforms from the trained rPPG-Fusion model (Fusion Siamese Contrast-Phys+ model) and the trained Respiratory-Fusion model (Waveform fusion model) for cognitive load prediction.

---

**Q6. From Table 4, it seems that blink markers have a large contribution to the performance. The performance of remote PPG + Remote Resp + Blink Markers is the best. I am curious about the performance of contact physiological signal + Blink Makers (contact PPG + contact Resp + blink markers).**

Ans: Thank you for this insightful question about the contribution of blink markers when combined with contact-based physiological signals. Following your suggestion, we conducted the requested experiment combining Contact PPG + Contact Resp + Blink Markers. The results show that this combination achieves 90.0% accuracy (F1: 0.905) with the MLP model, and 82.50% accuracy (F1: 0.837) with Gradient Boosting (GB), which indeed outperforms the best remote result of 86.49% accuracy (F1: 0.878) using Remote PPG + Remote Resp + Blink Markers with GB. The strong performance confirms that blink markers provide valuable cognitive load information regardless of whether they're combined with contact or remote physiological signals. 

The similar performance between contact-based multimodal (90.0%) and remote-based multimodal (86.49%) approaches demonstrates that our remote sensing pipeline can achieve near-equivalent results to traditional contact methods. We note that the contact+blink combination was evaluated on 40 samples, while the remote+blink combination used 37 samples (due to corrupted camera/radar recordings). This slight difference in sample size may contribute to the performance variation. 

The detailed **sample counts (low load, high load)** are in the table below:
| Set   | Patients | Contact (PPG, Resp) + Blink | Remote(PPG, Resp) + Blink |
|-------|----------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Train | 25       | 100 (50 low, 50 high)       | 93 (43 low, 50 high)        |
| Val   | 2        | 8 (4 low, 4 high)           | 7 (3 low, 4 high)           |
| Test  | 10       | 40 (20 low, 20 high)        | 37 (17 low, 20 high)        |

This result strengthens our core finding that multimodal integration is key to robust cognitive load estimation. More importantly, it demonstrates that remote sensing can achieve comparable performance to contact-based approaches when integrated with complementary modalities like blink markers. This supports our vision of developing practical, non-intrusive cognitive monitoring systems.

summary.value:
This paper examines how non-contact ("remote") sensors such as RGB, near IR, and thermal cameras as well as RF(radar) waveforms can monitor vital signs and mental workload of human subjects in a laboratory setting.

Specifically, two predictive modeling goals are pursued:

1) predict physiological vital signs like heart rate, respitory rate, and blink rate from non-contact sensor signals
2) predict cognitive load (binary high/low) using *estimated* vital signs from step 1 as input features

*Data contribution*. To help the community achieve this goal, the paper contributes a dataset of 37 participants, each observed in a bespoke "seated in a cockpit" lab setup (see Fig 2) where they are monitored with several multi-modal sensors including remote sensors of primary interest as well as some contact sensors (chest band, pulse oximeter) to help establish ground truth labels.

Signals are recorded as the participants complete several 2-min tasks designed to induce low mental workload (tasks like 'sit still' or 'read') and high mental workload (2 tasks involving memorizing numbers then doing math problems)

*Benchmarking contribution*. Using this data, they propose a common task evaluation strategy (train on 25, validation on 2, test on 10 subjects) and develop benchmarks for vital sign regression (task 1 above) and cognitive load classification (task 2 above).

*Key findings*: Key takeaways are that (1) current pipelines seem to be high-quality for both HR and RR estimation (both MAE metrics suggest nearing saturation), (2) gradient-boosted ensembles of trees with hand-crafted features seem to beat deep learning for cognitive load classification from HR/RR/blnking proxy inputs.

strengths_contributions.value:
## Significance / originality

This dataset seems positioned to be an authoritative benchmark for multimodal sensor-based estimation of cognitive load. There's plenty of interest in these tasks in the community, so I have a favorable assessment of potential significance.

For originality, Table 1 shows good evidence that this new dataset offers new features (in terms of multi-modality and "true labels") not available in past work. I feel convinced this work clears the bar in terms of novelty, though I don't work directly in this area.

## Experimental Quality

There's lots to appreciate about the quality of experiments:

* setup of the evaluation (using a split-by-subject train/val/test design) is well-done to assess generalization potential to new subjects
* scope of sensor combinations assessed seems valuable
* scope of different ML pipelines assessed seems reasonable
* performance metrics are suitable
* detailed interpretation of each experiment's results is appreciated for nuance (e.g. how the MAE for RR was observed to be generally closer due to scale of typical RR measurement)

limitations_weaknesses.value:
## Potential issues in data collection/curation

### DC1: Rationale for estimating cognitive load from heart/respiration/eye signals needs more justification

The story in the introduction suggests that heart/breathing/blinking signals can be used to estimate cognitive workload. This partially makes sense to me, but I suggest the authors should *justify* why this is mechanistically plausible, in the form of citations and brief summaries of the first-principles at work for each specific sensor. 

That is:

* why would heart rate relate to cognitive load?
* why would breathing relate to cognitive load?
* why would blinking relate to cognitive load?

I worry about whether these biosignals can truly predict *cognitive load* or if they can only predict confounding correlated constructs like *stress*. 

Consider the difference between:

* solving one digit by one digit multiplication problems at a demanding pace
* solving many-digit multiplication problems but at a relaxed pace

I'd (perhaps naively) argue the first is low-mental-effort but high stress, while the latter is high-effort, lower stress. Would heart rate or blinking really be able to distinguish the mental effort here?

### DC2: Is the label being captured really cognitive load? Or a correlated construct like stress?

The "ground truth" measurement of cognitive load is obtained from *adding together*  self-reported TLX scores for *mental*, *stress*, and *effort*. Is this adding together a common approach in the literature to define a cognitive load score? What's the rationale for doing this? I partially worry that the stress score is what would be more easily predicted by HR/RR/blinking. Would results change much if you only used the *mental* TLX score?

This study also doesn't seem able to distinguish stress and mental TLX responses... there isn't a task/activity designed to induce high stress but low mental work, or vice versa. 


### DC3: Lack of direct contact sensor for cognitive load

One limitation in this work is the "truth" for cognitive load comes from a combination of task design and self-reported TLX scores. This means there's only a high-level gist for each 2 minute session, rather than detailed moment-by-moment assessment. Contact sensors like EEG or fNIRS could have been used to assess physiological proxies of cognitive load (brain activity) more directly and in more fine-grained fashion, but that was not done in the study. Probably for obvious reasons (budget, intrusiveness, not 100% reliable).

I don't see this as a show-stopper at all, but just a potential limitation that is worth discussion and a nod to potential future work.


## Potential issues in ML experiments

### E1: Setup of supervised learning tasks needs more description

For each prediction task, the main paper needs to provide more concrete details about the input/output pairs used to train models. 

For the vital sign regression tasks: 

* Are you predicting one HR/RR/blink value for each 2 min task? Or do you break each task into smaller time windows and predict a separate value for each?
* What is assumed about the frequency / duration of each input sensor signal?
* How exactly do you get "truth" for each input window? Where in time to truth values come from, and how is pooling achieved? (e.g. do you predict the average HR observed in the 2 min window)?

For the cognitive load classification task:

* What is assumed about the frequency / duration of each input sensor signal? 2 min windows? Shorter, more frequency windows?
* What is the class-balance of high/low categories? Hard to know if accuracy of 75% is "good" or "bad" without this.
* Are high load instances all from the numbers/patterns task?

I'd recommend a careful rewrite of Sec 4.1 and 4.2 to carefully describe in order:

* how the prediction task is set up
* what methods are used and why
* any key details about training / method setup
* how hyperparameters were selected

### E2: Results reporting needs statistical uncertainty / significance testing

For all tasks, but especially cognitive load classification and RR regression, some kind of uncertainty quantification about performance metrics would be valuable. 

It is also important for benchmarks to help establish how an ML pipeline would be justified as "significantly better" than another pipeline.  For the binary clf evaluations, I might suggest looking at bootstrap samples of accuracy differences, where the bootstrap specifically resamples which subjects are included in the test set.


### E3: Use of validation set and hyperparameter tuning strategy needs more detail.

There's clearly a dedicated validation set, but its use is not obvious from reading the main paper. Is this used for hyperparameter search? Early stopping?

In general, ML methods are well-known to be quite sensitive to hyperparameters... especially where deep learning is vulnerable to overfitting (as in cognitive load experiments), I wonder what was done to mitigate overfitting? Describing the hyperparameter learning/search strategy in more detail would be valuable.

ethical_considerations.value: Yes, there are ethics concerns that require attention by the authors

ethical_comments.value:
Study mentions they have IRB approval with clearly stated approval document number. This is much appreciated.

My *privacy/consent* based concern is: Since we have RGB camera data of subject faces, is there a risk of reidentification? I assume this was handled by the IRB review, but given public release I'd just want some confirmation from the authors about how subjects knew their full face would be released to the public and consented to this.

dataset_code_comments.value: I looked quickly at the shared code (on github) and data link (on box)... it does seem to be accessible and offers documentation about reproducibility that seems followable. I only skimmed quickly, but I have no major concerns yet.

additional_feedback.value:
### Questions 


1) How do the TLX self-assessment surveys fit into the chronology of the task sequence during data collection? Do they pause after each 2 min task to take a short survey? Do they complete a TLX survey at the end of everything? 

2) Did you confirm that all participants actually engaged in the high-workload tasks? For example, they answered mostly correctly (or got close) with the intermediate multiplication problems? Were there criteria to discard recordings of the subject didn't engage?

### Limitations

I think current main paper could use expanded discussion of several limitations:

* what the 'ground truth' labels really measure (stress/effort vs cognitive load)
* current labeled dataset doesn't seem to be able to distinguish mental work from stress levels, given how labels are formed and what the background task design is
* what expected ceiling is in terms of how well remote sensors could ever hope to do for cognitive load. Do we think there would always be a gap between contact and non-contact sensors?
* what might change if we gathered *even more* data from more subjects? would we expect deep learning to outperform hand-crafted features?
* Acknowledge that this work only looks at average performance. Are there some subjects where performance is much worse? 

### Minor suggestions

In addition to citing work on EEG, the authors might consider citing other work on other contact sensors (like fNIRS) for cognitive load, to help readers get a big picture of the literature. 

The 'hand-engineered' features in Sec 5.1 are interesting... is there prior work to cite that suggested these features?

final_justification.value: I still lean accept on this one. I think with promised revisions will be a nice paper.

summary.value: The CogPhys dataset introduced in this work offers well-constructed multimodal dataset (RGB, NIR, thermal, and RF) for benchmarking remote physiological sensing methods (HR and RR) as well as cognitive load classification. The dataset includes ground-truth physiological signals using contact-based sensors along with NASA-TLX survey-based user responses for cognitive estimation. It uniquely enables estimating cognitive load using multimodal contactless sensing methods, and signifies the effectiveness of eye-blink waveforms. In addition to the dataset, the paper contributes a method (Siamese variant of ContrastPhys+ model (Fusion model) ) and a benchmarking assessment of DL and feature-engineered ML models for contactless estimation of cognitive load.

strengths_contributions.value:
* The paper is well-written and easy to follow. 
* This work presents effective experimental design and acquisition protocol allowing systematic comparison of contact-based and remote physiological sensing menthods for cognitive load assessment. 
* The dataset size is at-par with existing rPPG datasets. It comprise multimodal data (RGB, NIR, thermal, and RF) along with ground-truth contact-based signals as well as subjective assessment of cognitive load from 37 participants.
* Authors have provided extensive benchmarking results for their introduced CogPhys dataset.
* Experiments with fusion model highlight the usefulness of multimodal imaging inputs in reliable estimation of physiological signals.
* Furthermore the contribution of blink-rate waveform, and effectiveness of feature-engineered ML model provides insights to achieving reliable cognitive load assessment through contactless methods.
* Overall, this work makes significant contributions, enabling researchers focusing on remote physiological sensing to build upon the benchmarks established for contactless HR, RR and cognitive load assessment using multimodal data.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
**Experimental Design and Dataset**

* It is unclear how synchronization was ensured between multiple contact-based and contactless data-streams. 

* Please provide references that inspired the experimental design and the data-acquisition protocol.

* If usable ECG data was only collected from a subset of participants, and if this subset is too small, removing this small subset can make a coherent dataset, alternatively, if this subset is large, specific details can be added to ReadMe highlighting the list of participants for whom ECG was not acquired.


**Data Preprocessing and Evaluation Method**

* In 4.1, although authors mention the use of rPPG-Toolbox and Contrast-Phys+ code repositories, and have shared the code, it is recommended to describe pre-processing steps for video frames. Some of these include - the spatial resolution of RGB and Thermal frames, number of epochs, and hyperparameters used to train each model. Please clarify if video frames were uniformly preprocessed for all models, and whether a frame-difference, as recommended by prior research [1], for eliminating stationary components, was used  across all model for RGB/ NIR/ Thermal?. 

* It is unclear if all benchmarking models were trained using the training-split comprising 25 participants, or existing pretrained weights of benchmarking models trained on other datasets were used.

* It is recommended to benchmark cross-dataset generalization of Fusion model for multimodal remote physiological signal extraction, e.g. evaluating the model trained on CogPhys using MMSE (HR and RR), and iBVP (HR) datasets. SCAMPS dataset [2] can be additionally used for training purpose.

* For the subject-wise split of 25/2/10, please explain how was this split defined, and how was validation set used for training Fusion Model, as well as ML and DL models for cognitive load classification. Concern: Selecting a model based on the validation set comprising 2 participants may be unreliable.

**Resuls, statistical significance and performance metrics** 

* Authors have marked "NA" for "Experiment statistical significance", however, it is recommended to evaluate the statistical significance for both method and benchmarking contributions. It is recommended to perform multi-fold analysis for fair evaluation of both - Fusion Model for physiological signal estimation and ML and DL models for cognitive load classification. 

* In addition, for each reported metrics (MAE, RMSE, MAPE and correlation), including standard error for each of these metrics (that rPPG-Toolbox already supports) can offer insights into the variance of each methods. 

* For Table 4, although, there is significant merit in Remote PPG + Remote Resp + Blink Markers, it will be very helpful to add a comparison with Contact PPG + Contact Resp + Blink Markers. Have authors evaluated this combination, specifically with ECG derived HRV, instead of PPG derived PRV [3]. 

* For results that compare HR and RR estimation benchmarking methods, it is highly recommended to report SNR and MACC (maximum amplitude of cross-correlation) [4], as these enable directly assessing model performance with estimated signals.


**Checklist**
* Safeguards: the question states - "Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible
release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse". Author's response about IRB approval does not fully address - how the misuse of the data will be safeguarded. Authors are requested to specify the license terms for the data usage and data sharing mechanism to address this.

[1] Chen, Weixuan, and Daniel McDuff. "Deepphys: Video-based physiological measurement using convolutional attention networks." Proceedings of the european conference on computer vision (ECCV). 2018.

[2] McDuff, Daniel, et al. "Scamps: Synthetics for camera measurement of physiological signals." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (2022): 3744-3757.

[3] Mejía-Mejía, Elisa, et al. "Heart rate variability (HRV) and pulse rate variability (PRV) for the assessment of autonomic responses." Frontiers in physiology 11 (2020): 779.

[4] Jitesh Joshi and Youngjun Cho. iBVP Dataset: Rgb-thermal rppg dataset with high resolution signal quality labels. Electronics, 13(7):1334, 2024.

dataset_code_comments.value:
Both the dataset and code are readily accessible. 

However, pretrained weights of models trained on 25-participant training set were not found at this expected code path -> CogPhys/final_model_release/. Authors are requested to include these pretrained weights for reproducibility.

additional_feedback.value:
* In addition to showing $Mean \Delta bpm$ in Figure-5 (right), it would be helpful to show a figure with actual distribution of HR and RR to highlight the diverse physiological states that this data may represent.

* Table 3 - reports HRV metrics (IBI), however it is unclear if the values reported in the table are MAE/ RMSE/ MAPE. Although supplementary data does mention this as MAE, please revise the column heading to reflect the same.

* In Table 6, for Features column, instead of mentioning 25+, 15+, 35+ and 50+, it will be helpful to clearly state the number of features used, and provide the specifics in the supplementary. 

* Few typographic errors exist in the paper - proof-reading is recommended to address the same.

title.value: CogPhys: Assessing Cognitive Load via Multimodal Remote and Contact-based Physiological Sensing

TLDR.value: A multimodal dataset to sense cognitive load via remote vitals sign extraction from camera and radar sensors.

abstract.value: Remote physiological sensing is an evolving area of research. As systems approach clinical precision, there is increasing focus on complex applications such as cognitive state estimation. Hence, there is a need for large datasets that facilitate research into complex downstream tasks such as remote cognitive load estimation. A first-of-its-kind, our paper introduces an open-source multimodal multi-vital sign dataset consisting of concurrent recordings from RGB, NIR (near-infrared), thermal, and RF (radio-frequency) sensors alongside contact-based physiological signals, such as pulse oximeter and chest bands, providing a benchmark for cognitive state assessment. By adopting a multimodal approach to remote health sensing, our dataset and its associated hardware system excel at modeling the complexities of cognitive load. Here, cognitive load is defined as the mental effort exerted during tasks such as reading, memorizing, and solving math problems. By using the NASA-TLX survey, we set personalized thresholds for defining high/low cognitive levels, enabling a more reliable benchmark. Our benchmarking scheme bridges the gap between existing remote sensing strategies and cognitive load estimation techniques by using vital signs (such as photoplethysmography (PPG) and respiratory waveforms) and physiological signals (blink waveforms) as an intermediary. Through this paper, we focus on replacing the need for intrusive contact-based physiological measurements with more user-friendly remote sensors. Our benchmarking demonstrates that multimodal fusion significantly improves remote vital sign estimation, with our fusion model achieving $<3~BPM$ (beats per minute) error for vital sign estimation. For cognitive load classification, the combination of remote PPG, remote respiratory signals, and blink markers achieves $86.49$% accuracy, approaching the performance of contact-based sensing ($87.5$%) and validating the feasibility of non-intrusive cognitive monitoring.
